claim: Microglia play key roles during prenatal development in defining neural circuitry function, including ensuring proper synaptic wiring and maintaining homeostasis.
source: Microglia, brain-resident macrophages, play key roles during prenatal development in defining neural circuitry function, including ensuring proper synaptic wiring and maintaining homeostasis.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific consensus about microglial function during development.

claim: Mammalian breathing rhythmogenesis arises from interacting brainstem neural networks that are assembled during embryonic development.
source: Mammalian breathing rhythmogenesis arises from interacting brainstem neural networks that are assembled during embryonic development, but the specific role of microglia in this process remains unknown.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about respiratory network development.

claim: The specific role of microglia in respiratory network assembly during embryonic development remains unknown.
source: Mammalian breathing rhythmogenesis arises from interacting brainstem neural networks that are assembled during embryonic development, but the specific role of microglia in this process remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: The parafacial respiratory group (epF) emerges at embryonic day (E) 14.5 in mice.
source: We first established the normal distribution of microglia within the wild-type (WT, Spi1+/+ (Pu.1 WT)) mouse (Mus musculus) brainstem at embryonic ages when the respiratory networks are known to emerge (embryonic day (E) 14.5 for the parafacial respiratory group (epF) and E16.5 for the preBötzinger complex (preBötC)).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and cited in the introduction.

claim: The preBötzinger complex (preBötC) emerges at E16.5 in mice.
source: We first established the normal distribution of microglia within the wild-type (WT, Spi1+/+ (Pu.1 WT)) mouse (Mus musculus) brainstem at embryonic ages when the respiratory networks are known to emerge (embryonic day (E) 14.5 for the parafacial respiratory group (epF) and E16.5 for the preBötzinger complex (preBötC)).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and cited in the introduction.

claim: Spontaneous respiratory-related activity in Spi1−/− embryos shows an abnormally slow rhythm frequency expressed by the epF at E14.5.
source: Spontaneous respiratory-related activity recorded from reduced in vitro preparations showed an abnormally slow rhythm frequency expressed by the epF at E14.5, the preBötC at E16.5, and in the phrenic motor nerves from E16.5 onwards.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging and electrophysiological recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Spontaneous respiratory-related activity in Spi1−/− embryos shows an abnormally slow rhythm frequency expressed by the preBötC at E16.5.
source: Spontaneous respiratory-related activity recorded from reduced in vitro preparations showed an abnormally slow rhythm frequency expressed by the epF at E14.5, the preBötC at E16.5, and in the phrenic motor nerves from E16.5 onwards.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Spontaneous respiratory-related activity in Spi1−/− embryos shows an abnormally slow rhythm frequency in the phrenic motor nerves from E16.5 onwards.
source: Spontaneous respiratory-related activity recorded from reduced in vitro preparations showed an abnormally slow rhythm frequency expressed by the epF at E14.5, the preBötC at E16.5, and in the phrenic motor nerves from E16.5 onwards.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from phrenic nerve recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Spi1−/− embryos have a reduced number of active epF neurons.
source: These deficits were associated with a reduced number of active epF neurons, defects in commissural projections that couple the bilateral preBötC half-centers, and an accompanying decrease in their functional coordination.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical staining and calcium imaging data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Spi1−/− embryos have defects in commissural projections that couple the bilateral preBötC half-centers.
source: These deficits were associated with a reduced number of active epF neurons, defects in commissural projections that couple the bilateral preBötC half-centers, and an accompanying decrease in their functional coordination.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical labeling data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Spi1−/− embryos show a decrease in functional coordination between bilateral preBötC half-centers.
source: These deficits were associated with a reduced number of active epF neurons, defects in commissural projections that couple the bilateral preBötC half-centers, and an accompanying decrease in their functional coordination.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings from bilateral preBötC networks presented in Figure 5.

claim: E18.5 Spi1−/− embryos are unable to sustain breathing activity ex utero.
source: These abnormalities probably contribute to eventual neonatal death, since plethysmography revealed that E18.5 Spi1−/− embryos are unable to sustain breathing activity ex utero.
evidence: This is supported by plethysmographic recordings presented in Figure 7.

claim: The abnormalities in respiratory networks probably contribute to eventual neonatal death in Spi1−/− embryos.
source: These abnormalities probably contribute to eventual neonatal death, since plethysmography revealed that E18.5 Spi1−/− embryos are unable to sustain breathing activity ex utero.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed breathing deficits and known lethality of the mutant.

claim: Microglia contribute to the proper establishment of the central respiratory command during embryonic development.
source: Our results thus point to a crucial contribution of microglia in the proper establishment of the central respiratory command during embryonic development.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Microglia play important roles in different aspects of the development of brain structures by controlling cell death, angiogenesis, synapse refining, neurogenesis, and axon tract formation.
source: Indeed, it is now established that microglia play important roles in different aspects of the development of brain structures by controlling cell death, angiogenesis, synapse refining, neurogenesis, and axon tract formation (Paolicelli et al., 2011; Thion and Garel, 2017; Li and Barres, 2018; Stevens and Schafer, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The preBötzinger complex (preBötC) is responsible for inspiration.
source: The two main brainstem neuronal groups involved in respiratory rhythmogenesis and motor burst activity phasing are the preBötzinger complex (preBötC) responsible for inspiration (Smith et al., 1991; Gray et al., 2001) and the parafacial respiratory group (pFRG), involved in pre-inspiration and active expiration, as well as in playing a crucial role in central chemoception (Onimaru and Homma, 2003; Guyenet et al., 2019; Pisanski et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The parafacial respiratory group (pFRG) is involved in pre-inspiration and active expiration.
source: The two main brainstem neuronal groups involved in respiratory rhythmogenesis and motor burst activity phasing are the preBötzinger complex (preBötC) responsible for inspiration (Smith et al., 1991; Gray et al., 2001) and the parafacial respiratory group (pFRG), involved in pre-inspiration and active expiration, as well as in playing a crucial role in central chemoception (Onimaru and Homma, 2003; Guyenet et al., 2019; Pisanski et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The parafacial respiratory group (pFRG) plays a crucial role in central chemoception.
source: The two main brainstem neuronal groups involved in respiratory rhythmogenesis and motor burst activity phasing are the preBötzinger complex (preBötC) responsible for inspiration (Smith et al., 1991; Gray et al., 2001) and the parafacial respiratory group (pFRG), involved in pre-inspiration and active expiration, as well as in playing a crucial role in central chemoception (Onimaru and Homma, 2003; Guyenet et al., 2019; Pisanski et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: An operational pFRG emerges first at embryonic day (E) 14.5 in mice.
source: The initial formation of these circuits occurs early during development: in mice, an operational pFRG emerges first at embryonic day (E) 14.5 (hence named embryonic parafacial group (epF) at this stage; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009) whereas the preBötC becomes active at E15.5 (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The preBötC becomes active at E15.5 in mice.
source: The initial formation of these circuits occurs early during development: in mice, an operational pFRG emerges first at embryonic day (E) 14.5 (hence named embryonic parafacial group (epF) at this stage; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009) whereas the preBötC becomes active at E15.5 (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: From E15.5 onwards, the epF and preBötC rhythmic bilateral networks are functionally and reciprocally connected.
source: From this latter stage onwards, these rhythmic bilateral networks are functionally and reciprocally connected, and the various respiratory motoneuronal pools are driven through complex ipsi- and contralateral projections (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2005; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009; Ruffault et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Respiratory motoneuronal pools are driven through complex ipsi- and contralateral projections.
source: From this latter stage onwards, these rhythmic bilateral networks are functionally and reciprocally connected, and the various respiratory motoneuronal pools are driven through complex ipsi- and contralateral projections (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2005; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009; Ruffault et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The Spi1−/− mutant mouse exhibits a complete absence of microglial cells in the nervous system.
source: The Spi1 mouse strain, exhibiting a complete absence of microglial cells in the nervous system (Back et al., 2004), was maintained and bred in our animal housing facility.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and confirmed by immunostaining data in Figure 1.

claim: Microglia were found present in brainstem tissue throughout the developmental period from E14.5 to E18.5 in wild-type mice.
source: Microglia were found present in brainstem tissue throughout this developmental period (Figure 1A, F, K), with an uneven distribution characterized by a preferential localization in motoneuronal pools, such as the facial (Figure 1B, G, L) and hypoglossal nuclei (Figure 1D, I, N).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Microglia show preferential localization in motoneuronal pools, such as the facial and hypoglossal nuclei.
source: Microglia were found present in brainstem tissue throughout this developmental period (Figure 1A, F, K), with an uneven distribution characterized by a preferential localization in motoneuronal pools, such as the facial (Figure 1B, G, L) and hypoglossal nuclei (Figure 1D, I, N).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Selective concentrations of microglia in loci where the respiratory generators are located were not observed.
source: In contrast, selective concentrations of microglia in loci where the respiratory generators are located, ventral to the facial nucleus in the case of the epF (Figure 1B, G, L) and ventrolateral to the nucleus ambiguus for the preBötC (Figure 1C, H, M) were not observed.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: A pronounced congregation of microglia flanking the two sides of the hindbrain midline was detected at all three developmental stages (E14.5, E16.5, E18.5).
source: However, in all three developmental stages we detected a pronounced congregation of microglia flanking the two sides of the hindbrain midline (Figure 1E, J, O).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Brainstem preparations from Spi1−/− embryos at E18.5 were completely devoid of Iba1 labeling at all rostro-caudal levels examined.
source: As expected, nervous tissue from such mutant embryos was completely devoid of labeling at all rostro-caudal levels examined (Figure 1P–T, see also Figures 4 and 5), including those regions in close proximity to brainstem motor nuclei and along the midline.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Higher concentrations of microglial cells are located at loci corresponding to the facial and hypoglossal nuclei.
source: Together with the subsequent construction of density maps from the GFP signal for microglia (Figure 2D, H, L), our data confirmed that higher concentrations of microglial cells are located at loci corresponding to the facial (Figure 2D) and hypoglossal nuclei (Figure 2H), as well as along the midline (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by 3D imaging and density mapping data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Higher concentrations of microglial cells are located along the midline.
source: Together with the subsequent construction of density maps from the GFP signal for microglia (Figure 2D, H, L), our data confirmed that higher concentrations of microglial cells are located at loci corresponding to the facial (Figure 2D) and hypoglossal nuclei (Figure 2H), as well as along the midline (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by 3D imaging and density mapping data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The total number of epF neurons was significantly decreased by 31% in Spi1−/− preparations compared to WT preparations at E14.5.
source: Specifically, from counts of all Phox2b+/Islet1,2− cells in the epF region (ventral to the facial nucleus) of slices containing Phox2b+/Islet1,2+ facial motoneurons, the total number of epF neurons was found to be significantly decreased by 31% in the mutants, from a mean of 477 ± 36 cells in WT preparations (n = 6) to 285 ± 19 cells in Spi1−/− preparations (p = 0.002; n = 5; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data from immunostained preparations shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is a significant reduction in the rostro-caudal extension of the facial nuclei in Spi1−/− preparations compared to WT preparations at E14.5.
source: In addition, we also observed a significant reduction in the rostro-caudal extension of the facial nuclei in Spi1−/− preparations compared to WT preparations, from 436 ± 7 µm in WT (n = 11) to 380 ± 8 µm in Spi1−/− hindbrains (n = 11; p < 0.001; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical measurements from immunostained preparations shown in Figure 3.

claim: In WT preparations at E14.5, epF cells generate rhythmic fluorescence fluctuations at a mean frequency of 12.4 ± 0.9 calcium transients/min.
source: In eight WT preparations, a column of cells generating rhythmically organized fluorescence fluctuations corresponding to neuronal impulse burst activity and occurring at a mean frequency of 12.4 ± 0.9 calcium transients/min were recorded in the region of the epF (Figure 3E, F).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Lowering the pH from 7.4 to 7.2 increases the cycle frequency of epF fluorescence signals to 18.7 ± 1 calcium transients/min in WT preparations at E14.5.
source: Moreover, when preparations (n = 4) were superfused by an artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF) solution with a lowered pH (decreased from 7.4 to 7.2), the cycle frequency of ongoing fluorescence signals increased to 18.7 ± 1 calcium transients/min (p = 0.002), as expected due to the known intrinsic sensitivity of the epF network to acidosis (Figure 3F; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data under different pH conditions shown in Figure 3.

claim: In Spi1−/− preparations at E14.5, the spontaneous epF network rhythm is generated at a significantly reduced cycle frequency of 8.2 ± 0.7 calcium transients/min compared to WT control.
source: In addition, the spontaneous epF network rhythm monitored under control aCSF was generated at a significantly reduced cycle frequency compared to WT control of 8.2 ± 0.7 calcium transients/min (p = 0.003; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The epF network's sensitivity to pH changes is conserved in the Spi1−/− mutant at E14.5.
source: On the other hand, the network's sensitivity to pH changes was conserved in the mutant, since reducing the aCSF pH to 7.2 induced a significant frequency increase to 14.4 ± 1.5 calcium transients/min (p = 0.001; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data under different pH conditions shown in Figure 3.

claim: The absence of microglia during embryonic development leads to both anatomical and functional abnormalities in the epF network at E14.5.
source: Together these findings indicate that the absence of microglia during embryonic development leads to both anatomical and functional abnormalities in the epF network at E14.5, although its chemosensitivity to acidosis is maintained.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical and functional data presented for the epF network.

claim: The chemosensitivity to acidosis of the epF network is maintained in Spi1−/− embryos at E14.5.
source: Together these findings indicate that the absence of microglia during embryonic development leads to both anatomical and functional abnormalities in the epF network at E14.5, although its chemosensitivity to acidosis is maintained.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing pH responsiveness in Figure 3.

claim: Rhythmic burst activity at the locus of the preBötC network occurs spontaneously in all E16.5 slice preparations tested, irrespective of genotype.
source: Such population recordings from E16.5 WT (n = 6) and Spi1−/− (n = 7) slices (Figure 4A, B) revealed the spontaneous occurrence of rhythmic burst activity at the locus of the preBötC network in all preparations tested, irrespective of genotype.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: PreBötC activity is generated at a significantly reduced cycle frequency in Spi1−/− preparations (5.5 ± 0.4 bursts/min) compared to WT preparations (7.6 ± 0.3 bursts/min) at E16.5.
source: Here again, this activity was generated at a significantly reduced cycle frequency in preparations from Spi1−/− embryos (5.5 ± 0.4 bursts/min) compared to 7.6 ± 0.3 bursts/min (p < 0.001) in WT preparations (Figure 4B, C), whereas the regularity of burst cycle periods remained comparable as indicated by the similar coefficients of variation in the two genotypes (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: The regularity of burst cycle periods in the preBötC remains comparable between WT and Spi1−/− preparations at E16.5.
source: Here again, this activity was generated at a significantly reduced cycle frequency in preparations from Spi1−/− embryos (5.5 ± 0.4 bursts/min) compared to 7.6 ± 0.3 bursts/min (p < 0.001) in WT preparations (Figure 4B, C), whereas the regularity of burst cycle periods remained comparable as indicated by the similar coefficients of variation in the two genotypes (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mean burst durations in the preBötC are significantly increased in Spi1−/− preparations (1.23 ± 0.03 s) compared to WT preparations (1.00 ± 0.02 s) at E16.5.
source: However, in addition to a lower frequency we also found a significant increase (p < 0.001) in the mean values of burst durations that varied from 1.23 ± 0.03 s in preparations obtained from Spi1−/− embryos (n = 7) compared to 1.00 ± 0.02 s in WT preparations (n = 6) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: Exposure to 0.5 µM Substance P induces a significant increase in the preBötC's rhythm frequency in both WT and Spi1−/− genotypes.
source: Exposure to 0.5 µM SP (as commonly used on such reduced embryonic preparations; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2005; Chevalier et al., 2016) induced a significant increase (p < 0.001) in the preBötC's rhythm frequency in both genotypes to 10.2 ± 0.6 bursts/min in WT preparations (n = 4), and to 9.6 ± 0.6 bursts/min in Spi1−/− preparations (n = 4) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings with pharmacological treatment shown in Figure 4.

claim: The mutant's preBötC network is functional at E16.5 and remains sensitive to Substance P after having developed in a tissue environment devoid of microglia.
source: Overall these findings therefore indicated that despite generating a slower (albeit regular) burst rhythm composed of longer bursts, the mutant's preBötC network is clearly functional at E16.5 and remains sensitive to a major peptidergic neuromodulator after having developed in a tissue environment devoid of microglia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data showing rhythmic activity and SP responsiveness.

claim: Considerably less commissural fibers traverse the hindbrain midline in Spi1−/− mutants compared to WT at E16.5 to E18.5.
source: As illustrated in Figure 5A (four examples of each genotype), considerably less commissural fibers were found to traverse the hindbrain midline in mutants compared to WT (Figure 5A1, A2).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical labeling data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A significantly wider range of delays between bilateral preBötC bursts is observed in Spi1−/− preparations (48.9 ± 27.8 ms) compared to WT preparations (−4±11.7 ms) at E16.5 to E18.5.
source: From measurements of the delay between the onset of a given preBötC network burst and that of its contralateral partner, in contrast to the strict synchrony of burst pairs in WT preparations, a significantly wider range of delays was observed in Spi1−/− preparations, with mean values attaining 48.9 ± 27.8 ms in the latter preparations compared to −4±11.7 ms in the former (Figure 5B2, B3; 15 bursts per preparation; p < 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by bilateral electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the absence of microglia during embryonic development, commissural projections between the bilateral preBötC networks develop abnormally.
source: Thus, in the absence of microglia during embryonic development, commissural projections between the bilateral preBötC networks develop abnormally, likely underlying the observed weakened synchronization between the two oscillator half-centers, and in turn, to the generation of longer and less frequent bursts of respiratory-related activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical and functional data presented for commissural projections.

claim: Abnormal commissural projections likely underlie the observed weakened synchronization between the two preBötC oscillator half-centers.
source: Thus, in the absence of microglia during embryonic development, commissural projections between the bilateral preBötC networks develop abnormally, likely underlying the observed weakened synchronization between the two oscillator half-centers, and in turn, to the generation of longer and less frequent bursts of respiratory-related activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between anatomical and functional deficits.

claim: Weakened synchronization between preBötC half-centers leads to the generation of longer and less frequent bursts of respiratory-related activity.
source: Thus, in the absence of microglia during embryonic development, commissural projections between the bilateral preBötC networks develop abnormally, likely underlying the observed weakened synchronization between the two oscillator half-centers, and in turn, to the generation of longer and less frequent bursts of respiratory-related activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional consequences of reduced synchronization.

claim: Rhythmic motor bursts were detected in all 11 WT and 7 Spi1−/− preparations tested at E18.5.
source: Rhythmic motor bursts were detected in all 11 WT and 7 Spi1−/− preparations tested (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by phrenic nerve recordings shown in Figure 6.

claim: Fictive respiratory rhythms in Spi1−/− preparations at E18.5 are generated with a significantly lower frequency (10.6 ± 0.5 bursts/min) than those recorded from WT preparations (14 ± 0.4 bursts/min).
source: However, such fictive respiratory rhythms in mutant preparations were still generated with a significantly lower frequency than those recorded from WT preparations (Spi1−/−, 10.6 ± 0.5 bursts/min; WT, 14 ± 0.4 bursts/min, p < 0.001), (Figure 6B1), although again with a comparable rhythm regularity (p = 0.7; Figure 6B2).
evidence: This is supported by phrenic nerve recordings shown in Figure 6.

claim: Phrenic motor bursts exhibit longer durations in Spi1−/− preparations (948 ± 18 ms) compared to WT (843 ± 11 ms) at E18.5.
source: In addition, individual phrenic motor bursts exhibited longer durations in the mutant preparations (948 ± 18 ms) compared to WT (843 ± 11 ms, p < 0.001), (Figure 6B3).
evidence: This is supported by phrenic nerve recordings shown in Figure 6.

claim: In WT preparations at E18.5, lowering the pH from 7.4 to 7.2 accelerates phrenic motor bursts from 13.3 ± 0.6 to 17.4 ± 0.6 bursts/min.
source: Accordingly, in control WT preparations (n = 6), ongoing rhythmic motor bursts recorded from C4 roots were accelerated by lowering the pH (from 7.4 to 7.2) of the bathing aCSF from 13.3 ± 0.6 to 17.4 ± 0.6 bursts/min (p < 0.001; Figure 6C, left).
evidence: This is supported by phrenic nerve recordings under different pH conditions shown in Figure 6.

claim: In Spi1−/− preparations at E18.5, lowering the pH from 7.4 to 7.2 induces a significant increase in phrenic burst frequency from 10.1 ± 0.3 to 16.9±0.9 bursts/min.
source: Similarly, however, in mutant littermates (n = 5), an equivalent aCSF acidification also induced a significant increase in phrenic burst frequency from 10.1 ± 0.3 to 16.9±0.9 bursts/min (p < 0.001, Figure 6C, right).
evidence: This is supported by phrenic nerve recordings under different pH conditions shown in Figure 6.

claim: The final respiratory drive to phrenic motoneurons continues to express centrally detected pH changes in the Spi1−/− embryos at E18.5.
source: This finding therefore demonstrated that despite a reduced frequency and a diminished epF network, the final respiratory drive to phrenic motoneurons continues to express centrally detected pH changes in the Spi1−/− embryos at E18.5, further confirming that the central chemosensitive property of the epf network is preserved.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pH responsiveness data from phrenic nerve recordings.

claim: The central chemosensitive property of the epF network is preserved in Spi1−/− embryos at E18.5.
source: This finding therefore demonstrated that despite a reduced frequency and a diminished epF network, the final respiratory drive to phrenic motoneurons continues to express centrally detected pH changes in the Spi1−/− embryos at E18.5, further confirming that the central chemosensitive property of the epf network is preserved.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pH responsiveness data.

claim: Bursts of activity in one C4 root are strictly coordinated with those of the contralateral root in Spi1−/− mutants at E18.5, with a mean delay of 0.8 ± 4 ms.
source: Indeed, bursts of activity in one C4 root were strictly coordinated with those of the contralateral root, with a mean delay of 0.8 ± 4 ms in the Spi1−/− mutant (range from −51.8 to 142.4 ms; n = 5, 14 bursts per preparation), similar (p = 0.6) to that observed in WT preparations (mean: 2.07 ± 4.6 ms; range from −77.6 to 149.1 ms; n = 5, 15 bursts per preparation).
evidence: This is supported by bilateral phrenic nerve recordings shown in Figure 6.

claim: The bilateral synchronization of the central respiratory command to the two phrenic motor pools is unaffected by the absence of microglia in the Spi1−/− mutant at E18.5.
source: Thus, the bilateral synchronization of the central respiratory command to the two phrenic motor pools that derives from the epF and preBötC networks acting in combination is apparently unaffected by the absence of microglia in the Spi1−/− mutant at the late prenatal stage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the bilateral phrenic nerve recordings showing synchrony.

claim: 14 out of 15 WT embryos at E18.5 expressed sustained rhythmic breathing movements at a mean frequency of 102.4 ± 3 breaths/min.
source: Of the WT embryos, 14/15 animals expressed sustained rhythmic breathing movements in response to mechanical stimulation at a mean frequency of 102.4 ± 3 breaths/min (Figure 7A), whereas the remaining WT embryo failed to do so for an unknown reason.
evidence: This is supported by plethysmographic recordings shown in Figure 7.

claim: The vast majority (9/11) of Spi1−/− embryos at E18.5 never began to generate breathing movements.
source: In direct contrast, the vast majority (9/11) of the Spi1−/− embryos, although they initially expressed a heartbeat, never began to generate breathing movements as evidenced by a virtually flat trace in the plethysmograph recordings (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by plethysmographic recordings shown in Figure 7.

claim: Two Spi1−/− embryos at E18.5 expressed abnormal breathing behavior for only a few minutes but died rapidly thereafter.
source: The remaining two mutant embryos expressed abnormal breathing behavior for only a few minutes but died rapidly hereafter.
evidence: This is supported by plethysmographic observations.

claim: The anomalies that emerge in the central respiratory networks of Spi1−/− embryos during embryonic development in the absence of microglia are very likely to participate in causing death at birth.
source: Therefore, the anomalies that emerge in the central respiratory networks of Spi1−/− embryos during embryonic development in the absence of microglia are very likely to participate in causing death at birth, with at least one contributing factor being an inability to sustain active breathing movements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed breathing deficits and neonatal lethality.

claim: An inability to sustain active breathing movements is at least one contributing factor to death at birth in Spi1−/− embryos.
source: Therefore, the anomalies that emerge in the central respiratory networks of Spi1−/− embryos during embryonic development in the absence of microglia are very likely to participate in causing death at birth, with at least one contributing factor being an inability to sustain active breathing movements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the plethysmographic data showing lack of breathing.

claim: The complete absence of microglia during Spi1−/− mouse embryonic development results in major deficits of the neuronal networks responsible for breathing behavior.
source: Our findings reveal that the complete absence of microglia during Spi1−/− mouse embryonic development results in major deficits of the identified neuronal networks responsible for breathing behavior, specifically in relation to their ability to produce an effective central respiratory command.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Respiratory rhythmogenesis relies on an interaction between distinct neuronal groups located in separate regions of the brainstem.
source: Respiratory rhythmogenesis relies on an interaction between distinct neuronal groups located in separate regions of the brainstem, which normally become sequentially operational during embryogenesis to produce a stable respiratory-related rhythm from 3 days before birth (at E15.5) onwards (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Respiratory networks become sequentially operational during embryogenesis to produce a stable respiratory-related rhythm from E15.5 onwards.
source: Respiratory rhythmogenesis relies on an interaction between distinct neuronal groups located in separate regions of the brainstem, which normally become sequentially operational during embryogenesis to produce a stable respiratory-related rhythm from 3 days before birth (at E15.5) onwards (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: When developing in an environment devoid of microglia, respiratory networks continue to become functional at typical developmental stages, but exhibit anomalies that lead to the generation of an overall slower rhythm.
source: In examining the anatomical and functional characteristics of the two main respiratory neuronal groups (the epF and the preBötC networks) we found that when developing in an environment devoid of microglia, these networks continue to become functional at typical developmental stages, but exhibit anomalies that lead to the generation of an overall slower rhythm and a subsequent inability to sustain breathing behavior at birth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data from multiple developmental stages.

claim: Respiratory networks developing in an environment devoid of microglia exhibit a subsequent inability to sustain breathing behavior at birth.
source: In examining the anatomical and functional characteristics of the two main respiratory neuronal groups (the epF and the preBötC networks) we found that when developing in an environment devoid of microglia, these networks continue to become functional at typical developmental stages, but exhibit anomalies that lead to the generation of an overall slower rhythm and a subsequent inability to sustain breathing behavior at birth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the plethysmographic data showing breathing failure.

claim: The deficit in respiratory function is likely to arise from a lack of the normal influence of microglia in regulating cell numbers and the proper wiring of the brainstem circuits responsible for respiratory rhythmogenesis during prenatal development.
source: This deficit is likely to arise from a lack of the normal influence of microglia in regulating cell numbers and the proper wiring of the brainstem circuits responsible for respiratory rhythmogenesis during prenatal development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed anatomical and functional deficits.

claim: The centrally generated respiratory rhythm results in part from network interactions between the parafacial respiratory group (epF at embryonic stages) and the preBötC.
source: The centrally generated respiratory rhythm results in part from network interactions between the parafacial respiratory group (epF at embryonic stages) and the preBötC (Feldman et al., 2013), both of which are strongly connected to their contralateral counterparts via midline-crossing commissural projections (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The epF and preBötC are both strongly connected to their contralateral counterparts via midline-crossing commissural projections.
source: The centrally generated respiratory rhythm results in part from network interactions between the parafacial respiratory group (epF at embryonic stages) and the preBötC (Feldman et al., 2013), both of which are strongly connected to their contralateral counterparts via midline-crossing commissural projections (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The cycle frequency of respiratory activity is determined by the intrinsic rhythm generated by each half-center network and the strength of the homo- and hetero-network synaptic interactions.
source: Thus, the cycle frequency of respiratory activity is determined by (1) the intrinsic rhythm generated by each half-center network, and (2) the strength of the homo- (preBötC/preBötC; epF/epF) and hetero- (preBötC/epF) network synaptic interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge of network interactions.

claim: During embryonic development between E14.5 and E16.5, the epF progressively entrains the intrinsically slower preBötC network, thereby setting the overall respiratory rhythm to an intermediate cycle frequency.
source: During embryonic development these dual controlling processes are established between E14.5 and E16.5 (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009), a period during which the epF (intrinsically active at a higher frequency) progressively entrains the intrinsically slower preBötC network, thereby setting the overall respiratory rhythm to an intermediate cycle frequency (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: At the time of their respective emergence, each respiratory network in the mutant generates rhythmic activity at an abnormally low frequency.
source: Here, we find in the mutant that at the time of their respective emergence, each respiratory network generates rhythmic activity at an abnormally low frequency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data from both epF and preBötC networks.

claim: The lower frequency of the epF in the mutant is likely to be the consequence of a substantially diminished number of constituent neurons.
source: In the case of the epF, this lower frequency is likely to be the consequence of a substantially diminished number of constituent neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between reduced cell numbers and reduced frequency.

claim: For the preBötC network, anomalies in commissural projections connecting the two bilaterally distributed preBötC neuronal groups are likely to contribute to the slower rhythm generation.
source: For the preBötC network, anomalies in commissural projections connecting the two bilaterally distributed preBötC neuronal groups, resulting in a diminished inter-network synchronization, are likely to contribute to the slower rhythm generation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical and functional data for commissural projections.

claim: When the epF and preBötC networks become fully connected at E16.5, their intra- and inter-circuit anomalies result in a reduced frequency of the final respiratory command observed at the level of motor output.
source: Ultimately, when these networks become fully connected at E16.5, their intra- and inter-circuit anomalies result in a reduced frequency of the final respiratory command observed at the level of motor output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined effects of network deficits on motor output.

claim: Spi1−/− mortality at P0 probably results from multiple functional defaults that are not necessarily exclusively CNS related.
source: While Spi1−/− mortality at P0 probably results from multiple functional defaults that are not necessarily exclusively CNS related (Back et al., 2004), the cause of death is very unlikely related to an immune system deficiency or the development of septicemia that could have arisen due to the absence of microglia.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known phenotype of the mutant and citation to prior literature.

claim: The cause of death in Spi1−/− embryos is very unlikely related to an immune system deficiency or the development of septicemia.
source: While Spi1−/− mortality at P0 probably results from multiple functional defaults that are not necessarily exclusively CNS related (Back et al., 2004), the cause of death is very unlikely related to an immune system deficiency or the development of septicemia that could have arisen due to the absence of microglia.
evidence: This is speculation based on the timing of death and known biology.

claim: Peripheral causes are likely to be involved in the premature death of animals devoid of microglia.
source: In contrast, peripheral causes are likely to be involved in the premature death of animals devoid of microglia.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known expression pattern of Spi1.

claim: Spi1 is expressed in hematopoietic stem cells and common lymphoid progenitors impacting not only microglia but also meningeal, choroid plexus, and perivascular macrophages, as well as peripheral immune cells.
source: Indeed, Spi1 is expressed in hematopoietic stem cells and common lymphoid progenitors impacting not only microglia but also meningeal, choroid plexus, and perivascular macrophages, as well as peripheral immune cells (Goldmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: No premature death was observed in transgenic mice in which microglia depletion was specifically restricted to the CNS.
source: In a recent study, no premature death was observed in transgenic mice in which microglia depletion was specifically restricted to the CNS (Rojo et al., 2019), thus directly inferring peripheral deficits, possibly including developmental malformations of the upper airways, lungs and heart, as important contributors to neonatal death of Spi1−/− mutants.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Peripheral deficits, possibly including developmental malformations of the upper airways, lungs and heart, are important contributors to neonatal death of Spi1−/− mutants.
source: In a recent study, no premature death was observed in transgenic mice in which microglia depletion was specifically restricted to the CNS (Rojo et al., 2019), thus directly inferring peripheral deficits, possibly including developmental malformations of the upper airways, lungs and heart, as important contributors to neonatal death of Spi1−/− mutants.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with CNS-specific microglia depletion models.

claim: Major defaults in overall breathing movement control and/or anomalies in cardiorespiratory activity are very likely contributing significantly to the inability of perinatal Spi1 mutants to survive after birth.
source: Therefore, major defaults in overall breathing movement control (potentially also at the peripheral level) and/or anomalies in cardiorespiratory activity are very likely contributing significantly to the inability of perinatal Spi1 mutants to survive after birth.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed breathing deficits and known lethality.

claim: Microglia enter and invade the CNS early during development.
source: Microglia are known to enter and invade the CNS early during development (Mosser et al., 2017; Thion and Garel, 2017; Angelim et al., 2018), consistent with an important role in the initial stages of neuronal circuit assembly (Casano and Peri, 2015; Reemst et al., 2016; Mosser et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microglia play an important role in the initial stages of neuronal circuit assembly.
source: Microglia are known to enter and invade the CNS early during development (Mosser et al., 2017; Thion and Garel, 2017; Angelim et al., 2018), consistent with an important role in the initial stages of neuronal circuit assembly (Casano and Peri, 2015; Reemst et al., 2016; Mosser et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microglia exhibit a specific spatiotemporal distribution in the embryonic brain, with a characteristic uneven distribution that coincides with the localization of progenitor niches, loci where neurogenesis and cell division occur, near developing blood vessels and the formation of axonal tracts.
source: Moreover, microglia exhibit a specific spatiotemporal distribution in the embryonic brain, with a characteristic uneven distribution that coincides with the localization of progenitor niches, loci where neurogenesis and cell division also occur, near developing blood vessels and the formation of axonal tracts (Ashwell, 1991; Fantin et al., 2010; Verney et al., 2010; Hoshiko et al., 2012; Swinnen et al., 2013; Squarzoni et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the developing brainstem, microglia express a preferential spatial distribution, with a higher prevalence in hindbrain motor nuclei and along each side of the hindbrain midline.
source: Similarly, in the developing brainstem, we find that microglia also express a preferential spatial distribution, with a higher prevalence not only in hindbrain motor nuclei but also along each side of the hindbrain midline.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and 3D imaging data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Most brainstem circuits are bilaterally distributed, with their activities coordinated by commissural axonal projections that cross the midline.
source: This latter observation was of particular interest since most brainstem circuits are bilaterally distributed, with their activities coordinated by commissural axonal projections that cross the midline.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of brainstem circuit organization.

claim: A strict left/right synchronization of motor output is required to produce a coordinated drive to the left and right diaphragm muscles.
source: This is especially relevant for the central networks organizing the respiratory command, where a strict left/right synchronization of motor output is required to produce a coordinated drive to the left and right diaphragm muscles (Bouvier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The commissural connectivity between the central respiratory groups displays redundancy and is extremely complex.
source: The commissural connectivity between the central respiratory groups displays redundancy and is extremely complex.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of respiratory circuit connectivity.

claim: A bilateral co-activation of the two epF networks occurs as early as E14.5.
source: For example, a bilateral co-activation of the two epF networks occurs as early as E14.5, with synchronizing signals being conveyed through multiple, but still anatomically undefined commissural pathways (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Commissural interneurons between the two preBötC networks participate in the synchronization of bilaterally coordinated contractions of inspiratory effector muscles.
source: In addition, commissural interneurons, both between the two preBötC networks (Smith et al., 1991; Bouvier et al., 2010) and between the ventral respiratory groups (VRGs) that contain pre-motoneurons (Wu et al., 2017), participate in the synchronization of bilaterally coordinated contractions of inspiratory effector muscles.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The anatomical specificity of preBötC commissural connectivity requires the Slit/Robo signaling pathway.
source: At the level of the preBötC, this anatomical specificity requires the Slit/Robo signaling pathway (Bouvier et al., 2010), but might also involve microglia due to the latter's localization near the midline and their known participation in axonal tract formation elsewhere in the CNS (Pont-Lezica et al., 2014; Squarzoni et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microglia might be involved in preBötC commissural connectivity due to their localization near the midline and their known participation in axonal tract formation elsewhere in the CNS.
source: At the level of the preBötC, this anatomical specificity requires the Slit/Robo signaling pathway (Bouvier et al., 2010), but might also involve microglia due to the latter's localization near the midline and their known participation in axonal tract formation elsewhere in the CNS (Pont-Lezica et al., 2014; Squarzoni et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation based on microglial localization and known functions, supported by citations.

claim: Inter-preBötC network projections are considerably reduced in the Spi1−/− embryos.
source: Consistent with this idea, our findings show firstly, that inter-preBötC network projections are considerably reduced in the Spi1−/− embryos, and second, and correspondingly, in slice preparations isolating the preBötC networks from Spi1−/− embryos at E16.5, the normal functional synchronization between the rhythmogenic half-centers is diminished.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical labeling data presented in Figure 5.

claim: In slice preparations isolating the preBötC networks from Spi1−/− embryos at E16.5, the normal functional synchronization between the rhythmogenic half-centers is diminished.
source: Consistent with this idea, our findings show firstly, that inter-preBötC network projections are considerably reduced in the Spi1−/− embryos, and second, and correspondingly, in slice preparations isolating the preBötC networks from Spi1−/− embryos at E16.5, the normal functional synchronization between the rhythmogenic half-centers is diminished.
evidence: This is supported by bilateral electrophysiological recordings presented in Figure 5.

claim: The redundancy of midline-crossing commissures between other brainstem centers is sufficient to offset the weakened local connections between the preBötC half-centers, thereby enabling the coordination between the downstream left and right motor outputs in the Spi1−/− embryo to be maintained.
source: This apparent compensation is likely attributable to the redundancy of midline-crossing commissures between the other brainstem centers that are sufficient to offset the weakened local connections between the preBötC half-centers (Wu et al., 2017), thereby enabling the coordination between the downstream left and right motor outputs in the Spi1−/− embryo to be maintained.
evidence: This is an inference based on the maintained bilateral synchrony of phrenic output despite preBötC deficits, supported by citation.

claim: The decreased frequency of phrenic motor output is likely to be the direct consequence of the slower rhythmic command signal emanating from the interacting epF and preBötC networks.
source: On the one hand, the decreased frequency is likely to be the direct consequence of the slower rhythmic command signal emanating from the interacting epF and preBötC networks, both groups separately generating a respiratory-related rhythmic activity at an abnormally slow frequency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed slow frequencies at multiple levels of the respiratory network.

claim: The increase in motor burst duration could have arisen from a reduction in the coordination within the preBötC networks and between inspiratory interneurons and VRG pre-motoneurons.
source: On the other hand, the increase in motor burst duration could have arisen from a reduction in the coordination within the preBötC networks and between inspiratory interneurons and VRG pre-motoneurons.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed coordination deficits.

claim: Reduced coordination within the preBötC networks would lead to a less synchronized drive to target motoneurons and thus an overall increase in phrenic motor burst duration in each cycle.
source: This in turn would lead to a less synchronized drive to target motoneurons and thus an overall increase in phrenic motor burst duration in each cycle.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying increased burst duration.

claim: The phrenic motor nucleus itself might be affected in the mutant, especially in light of the finding that microglia are normally present in high density in the different brainstem motor nuclei.
source: Another possibility is that the phrenic motor nucleus itself is affected in the mutant, especially in light of our finding that microglia are normally present in high density in the different brainstem motor nuclei.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed microglial distribution in motor nuclei.

claim: When developing in the absence of microglia, the firing properties of motoneuronal groups, including those in the phrenic nucleus, might be directly affected, thereby contributing to the observed increase in phrenic burst duration.
source: Thus, when developing in the absence of microglia, the firing properties of these motoneuronal groups, including those in the phrenic nucleus, might be directly affected, thereby contributing to the observed increase in phrenic burst duration.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms underlying the observed phenotype.

claim: The essential regulation of neuronal numbers in the construction of neural circuitry during development occurs through several mechanisms in which microglia may participate: neuronal death, survival, and migration.
source: The essential regulation of neuronal numbers in the construction of neural circuitry during development occurs through several mechanisms in which microglia may participate: neuronal death, survival, and migration (Thion and Garel, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In the mouse respiratory system, epF neurons originate in the dB2 domain of rhombomere 5 (r5) then migrate conjointly with facial motoneurons to reach their final location in r6 by E14.5.
source: In the mouse respiratory system, epF neurons originate in the dB2 domain of rhombomere 5 (r5) then migrate conjointly with facial motoneurons to reach their final location in r6 by E14.5, near the ventral surface of the hindbrain and below the facial motor nucleus (Dubreuil et al., 2009; Ramanantsoa et al., 2011; Mellen and Thoby-Brisson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Perturbations in epF formation have been detected in different mouse lines genetically modified for transcription factors known to specify epF neuronal components, such as Phox2b, Egr2, Lbx1, and Atoh1.
source: Perturbations in epF formation have been detected in different mouse lines genetically modified for transcription factors known to specify epF neuronal components, such as Phox2b, Egr2, Lbx1, and Atoh1 (Pagliardini et al., 2008; Dubreuil et al., 2009; Rose et al., 2009; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009; Ruffault et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In most transcription factor mutant mouse lines, the number of epF neurons was found to be drastically reduced, with significant resultant effects on epF network function, including both rhythmogenesis and loss of CO2/pH responsiveness.
source: In most cases, the number of epF neurons was found to be drastically reduced in these mutant animal, with significant resultant effects on epF network function, including both rhythmogenesis and loss of CO2/pH responsiveness.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the Spi1−/−, the reduction of neurons constituting the epF group presumably results from an abnormally high level of epF cell death and/or migratory dysfunction.
source: In the Spi1−/−, the reduction (by ~31%) of neurons constituting the epF group presumably results from an abnormally high level of epF cell death and/or migratory dysfunction.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the reduced epF cell number.

claim: The diminished epF population size in Spi1−/− embryos probably explains the production of a slower epF rhythm at E14.5.
source: This diminished epF population size in turn probably explains the production of a slower (by 33%) epF rhythm at E14.5, and indeed, also that of fictive respiration observed from E16.5 onwards in isolated hindbrain preparations, where rhythmic burst activity in the phrenic motor roots arises from both the epF and the now active preBötC generators operating in combination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between reduced cell numbers and reduced frequency.

claim: At E16.5, the epF is known to entrain the preBötC.
source: Since at this later embryonic stage the epF is known to entrain the preBötC (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009), a slower intrinsic rhythm generated by the epF in the mutant will drive the preBötC at an equally reduced frequency (but note, the preBötC itself generates a slower rhythm; see below), with a resultant production of slower phrenic motor bursting.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A slower intrinsic rhythm generated by the epF in the mutant will drive the preBötC at an equally reduced frequency, with a resultant production of slower phrenic motor bursting.
source: Since at this later embryonic stage the epF is known to entrain the preBötC (Thoby-Brisson et al., 2009), a slower intrinsic rhythm generated by the epF in the mutant will drive the preBötC at an equally reduced frequency (but note, the preBötC itself generates a slower rhythm; see below), with a resultant production of slower phrenic motor bursting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known entrainment relationship and observed frequencies.

claim: The epF's intrinsic sensitivity to pH changes at E14.5 is preserved in the mutant.
source: In contrast, the epF's intrinsic sensitivity to pH changes at E14.5 is preserved in the mutant, indicating that despite a reduction in constituent neurons, the normal chemosensing capability of this neuronal group is preserved.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing pH responsiveness in Figure 3.

claim: Despite a reduction in constituent neurons, the normal chemosensing capability of the epF neuronal group is preserved in Spi1−/− embryos.
source: In contrast, the epF's intrinsic sensitivity to pH changes at E14.5 is preserved in the mutant, indicating that despite a reduction in constituent neurons, the normal chemosensing capability of this neuronal group is preserved.
evidence: This is an inference based on the preserved pH responsiveness.

claim: The epF's chemosensitivity property persists later in development, since acidifying the aCSF bathing isolated brainstem preparations at E18.5 still evoked a frequency increase of respiratory activity recorded at the level of phrenic roots.
source: This functional property also persists later in development, since acidifying the aCSF bathing isolated brainstem preparations at E18.5 still evoked a frequency increase of respiratory activity recorded at the level of phrenic roots.
evidence: This is supported by phrenic nerve recordings under different pH conditions shown in Figure 6.

claim: Although the complete neuronal composition of epF circuitry early during embryonic development depends on the presence of microglia, in the latter's absence the network's basic rhythmogenic and chemosensitivity properties remain.
source: Together these findings therefore indicate that although the complete neuronal composition of epF circuitry early during embryonic development depends on the presence of microglia, nevertheless, in the latter's absence the network's basic rhythmogenic and chemosensitivity properties remain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined anatomical and functional data for the epF network.

claim: The preBötC network originates from the V0v domain in r6/7.
source: The preBötC network originates from the V0v domain in r6/7, and is composed of a heterogeneous population of Dbx1-specified interneurons that migrate radially from their territory of origin (near the sulcus limitans bordering the fourth ventricle) to their final position in the ventro-lateral area in the vicinity of the nucleus ambiguus (Bouvier et al., 2010; Gray et al., 2010; Mellen and Thoby-Brisson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The preBötC network is composed of a heterogeneous population of Dbx1-specified interneurons that migrate radially from their territory of origin to their final position in the ventro-lateral area in the vicinity of the nucleus ambiguus.
source: The preBötC network originates from the V0v domain in r6/7, and is composed of a heterogeneous population of Dbx1-specified interneurons that migrate radially from their territory of origin (near the sulcus limitans bordering the fourth ventricle) to their final position in the ventro-lateral area in the vicinity of the nucleus ambiguus (Bouvier et al., 2010; Gray et al., 2010; Mellen and Thoby-Brisson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The preBötC network in the mutant is sufficiently preserved in its ability to produce inspiration-related rhythmic activity, albeit at a slower frequency.
source: However, our physiological results indicate that this network in the mutant is sufficiently preserved, if affected at all, in its ability to produce inspiration-related rhythmic activity, albeit at a slower frequency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological recordings showing rhythmic activity.

claim: The frequency reduction in the preBötC could result from a diminished connectivity between inspiratory interneurons as indicated by the reduced number of commissural projections between the preBötC half-centers.
source: This frequency reduction could result from a diminished connectivity between inspiratory interneurons as indicated by the reduced number of commissural projections between the preBötC half-centers (as discussed above) and a consequent less efficient synchronization between the two preBötC groups.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the frequency reduction.

claim: Microglia play a role in shaping and refining synapses during development.
source: Another plausible explanation resides with the known role of microglia in shaping and refining synapses during development (Thion and Garel, 2017; Thion et al., 2018), in their formation and maturation (Miyamoto et al., 2016), and in regulating synaptic activity (Ben Achour et al., 2010; Li et al., 2012; Pascual et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microglia play a role in synapse formation and maturation.
source: Another plausible explanation resides with the known role of microglia in shaping and refining synapses during development (Thion and Garel, 2017; Thion et al., 2018), in their formation and maturation (Miyamoto et al., 2016), and in regulating synaptic activity (Ben Achour et al., 2010; Li et al., 2012; Pascual et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microglia play a role in regulating synaptic activity.
source: Another plausible explanation resides with the known role of microglia in shaping and refining synapses during development (Thion and Garel, 2017; Thion et al., 2018), in their formation and maturation (Miyamoto et al., 2016), and in regulating synaptic activity (Ben Achour et al., 2010; Li et al., 2012; Pascual et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Multiple microglial influences might contribute to the establishment of the preBötC network, in which appropriate interneuronal connections and activity levels are required for proper respiratory rhythmogenesis.
source: Such multiple influences might also contribute to the establishment of the preBötC network, in which appropriate interneuronal connections and activity levels are required for proper respiratory rhythmogenesis.
evidence: This is speculation based on known microglial functions and observed preBötC deficits.

claim: Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF) modulates preBötC activity through an activation of Trkb receptors expressed by inspiratory neurons.
source: Of further relevance is the fact that Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF) is known to modulate preBötC activity through an activation of Trkb receptors expressed by inspiratory neurons and is required for the normal development of the central respiratory rhythm (Erickson et al., 1996; Balkowiec and Katz, 1998; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2003; Bouvier et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: BDNF is required for the normal development of the central respiratory rhythm.
source: Of further relevance is the fact that Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF) is known to modulate preBötC activity through an activation of Trkb receptors expressed by inspiratory neurons and is required for the normal development of the central respiratory rhythm (Erickson et al., 1996; Balkowiec and Katz, 1998; Thoby-Brisson et al., 2003; Bouvier et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mice lacking BDNF display severe deficits in breathing control, including depressed ventilation and an irregular respiratory rhythm.
source: Indeed, mice lacking BDNF display severe deficits in breathing control, including depressed ventilation and an irregular respiratory rhythm.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge from prior literature.

claim: Microglia are able to release BDNF that can cause a disinhibition of neural circuits and increase network excitability.
source: On the other hand, microglia are able to release BDNF that can cause a disinhibition of neural circuits and increase network excitability (Coull et al., 2005; Trang et al., 2011; Ferrini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microglia might serve as a source of BDNF for the preBötC network, and whose absence during embryonic development leads to abnormal preBötC function.
source: A further possibility, therefore, is that microglia also serve as a source of BDNF for the preBötC network, and whose absence during embryonic development leads to abnormal preBötC function.
evidence: This is speculation based on known microglial BDNF release and preBötC BDNF requirements.

claim: The roles of microglia in neurogenesis, axonal tract formation, and proper circuit wiring are relevant to the developmental establishment of a functional central respiratory command.
source: The roles of microglia in neurogenesis, axonal tract formation, and proper circuit wiring are evidently relevant to the developmental establishment of a functional central respiratory command, as evidenced here by our Spi1−/− analysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed deficits in the Spi1−/− mutant.

claim: Despite anatomical and functional disturbances in respiratory network emergence, the absence of microglia during embryonic development does not totally prevent the formation of neural circuits capable of fundamental respiratory-related rhythmogenesis.
source: Nonetheless, despite anatomical and functional disturbances in respiratory network emergence, the absence of microglia during embryonic development does not totally prevent the formation of neural circuits capable of fundamental respiratory-related rhythmogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that rhythmic activity persists in the mutant.

claim: The persistence of respiratory rhythmogenesis in the absence of microglia is probably due to additional strong and even redundant mechanisms that contribute to establishing the integral central command for such a vital function.
source: This is probably due to additional strong and even redundant mechanisms that contribute to establishing the integral central command for such a vital function.
evidence: This is speculation about why respiratory rhythmogenesis persists despite microglial absence.

claim: The number and morphology of microglia throughout brain development are dependent upon the sex and age of an individual, as well as the particular brain region.
source: The number and morphology of microglia throughout brain development are dependent upon the sex and age of an individual, as well as the particular brain region (Schwarz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Sex-specific differences in microglial numbers and morphologies have only been found at postnatal stages.
source: So far, however, sex-specific differences in such parameters have only been found at postnatal stages, whereas in the prenatal period, brain microglia numbers and morphologies are apparently not affected by animal gender (Schwarz and Bilbo, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In the prenatal period, brain microglia numbers and morphologies are apparently not affected by animal gender.
source: So far, however, sex-specific differences in such parameters have only been found at postnatal stages, whereas in the prenatal period, brain microglia numbers and morphologies are apparently not affected by animal gender (Schwarz and Bilbo, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Microglia colonize the CNS early during embryogenesis and contribute to various developmental processes.
source: Microglia colonize the CNS early during embryogenesis and contribute to various developmental processes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior literature.

claim: The early roles of embryonic microglia include the regulation of axonal tract formation.
source: The early roles of embryonic microglia have only begun to be described in rodents, including the regulation of axonal tract formation (Pont-Lezica et al., 2014; Squarzoni et al., 2014), positioning of migratory interneurons (Squarzoni et al., 2014), modulation of neurogenesis and synapse refinement (for review see Witcher et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The early roles of embryonic microglia include positioning of migratory interneurons.
source: The early roles of embryonic microglia have only begun to be described in rodents, including the regulation of axonal tract formation (Pont-Lezica et al., 2014; Squarzoni et al., 2014), positioning of migratory interneurons (Squarzoni et al., 2014), modulation of neurogenesis and synapse refinement (for review see Witcher et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The early roles of embryonic microglia include modulation of neurogenesis and synapse refinement.
source: The early roles of embryonic microglia have only begun to be described in rodents, including the regulation of axonal tract formation (Pont-Lezica et al., 2014; Squarzoni et al., 2014), positioning of migratory interneurons (Squarzoni et al., 2014), modulation of neurogenesis and synapse refinement (for review see Witcher et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Microglia are implicated in a wide range of processes, rendering these cells important contributors to the assembly and refinement of central neuronal circuits during ontogenesis.
source: Thus, microglia are implicated in a wide range of processes, rendering these cells important contributors to the assembly and refinement of central neuronal circuits during ontogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the multiple known roles of microglia.

claim: The possible roles of microglia in breathing control have so far been mainly investigated in relation to inflammatory responsiveness and its impact on rhythm generation, autoresuscitation, chemoreception, and plasticity at postnatal ages.
source: In the context of breathing control, the possible roles of microglia have so far been mainly investigated in relation to inflammatory responsiveness and its impact on rhythm generation, autoresuscitation, chemoreception, and plasticity at postnatal ages (Huxtable et al., 2011; Huxtable et al., 2013; Tadmouri et al., 2014; Lorea-Hernández et al., 2016; Camacho-Hernández et al., 2019; Beyeler et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: This study provides new data on the contribution of microglia to the early anatomical and functional development of brainstem networks responsible for respiratory rhythmogenesis.
source: Here, in a first description of the distribution and role of microglia in the embryonic hindbrain, we provide new data on the contribution of microglia to the early anatomical and functional development of brainstem networks responsible for respiratory rhythmogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty and contribution of the current study.

claim: The findings underline the critical role played by microglia in the ontogeny of central neuronal circuits, including those controlling vital physiological functions.
source: Our findings thus underline the critical role played by these brain-resident macrophages in the ontogeny of central neuronal circuits, including those controlling vital physiological functions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all experimental data presented in the study.
